title: Halal Food in KL: Where to Eat and How to Check
metaDescription: Halal food in KL by area, from Masjid India to Bukit Bintang, and how to check a JAKIM halal certificate in the Halal Malaysia directory.

contentBlocks.content: Halal food in KL comes with labels that look alike but mean different things: a JAKIM halal certificate, a Muslim-owned kitchen, or a sign that says "no pork no lard". This guide shows you how Malaysia's halal certificate works, how to check a restaurant in the Halal Malaysia directory from your phone, and where to eat around Masjid India, KLCC, Chinatown and Bukit Bintang. For every place below, we say exactly what we could confirm on 5 November 2026.
Key Takeaways
Who certifies halal food in Malaysia? JAKIM, the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia, or a state Islamic religious department or council, known as JAIN or MAIN (Halal Malaysia).

What does the halal logo look like? An eight-pointed star inside a circle, the Arabic word حلال in the centre, "HALAL" below it, and "Malaysia" in Roman and Arabic letters around the edge (Halal Malaysia).
How do I check a restaurant? Search its name under Premis Makanan in the Verify Halal Status box on halal.gov.my, then check the outlet address and the expiry date (Halal Malaysia directory).

Is "no pork no lard" halal? It is not a certification. In August 2025 the Selangor Islamic Religious Department said such signs are prohibited for eateries without a halal certificate (The Straits Times).
Which places here are certified? Only the ones we found in the directory today, and we say so each time. Google Maps labels such as "Halal restaurant" are set by the business itself.
How halal certification works in Malaysia

Halal means permitted by Islamic law. In Malaysia the recognised authority is JAKIM, the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia, or the state Islamic religious department or council (JAIN or MAIN), whichever applies. Restaurants, food courts, cafés, kiosks and hotel restaurants all count as food premises and can apply for a certificate (Halal Malaysia).

The definition JAKIM uses, from the Trade Descriptions Order 1975, goes beyond the menu. Halal food contains no part of an animal that is forbidden to Muslims or was not slaughtered according to Islamic law, and nothing considered impure. It is not prepared with equipment that is not free of impurities, and it is not stored with or near food that fails those tests (Halal Malaysia). So a certificate covers the kitchen and the supply chain.

The logo is issued by JAKIM, JAIN or MAIN. It shows an eight-pointed star inside a circle, the Arabic word حلال in the star, "HALAL" in Roman letters below it, and "Malaysia" in Roman and Arabic letters around the circle, separated by two small five-pointed stars (Halal Malaysia). Save a picture of it on your phone before you fly so you can match it at the counter.
Halal certified, Muslim-owned, no pork no lard

Halal certified means the outlet holds a current certificate from JAKIM, JAIN or MAIN and shows up in the Halal Malaysia directory (Halal Malaysia directory). A certified kitchen has to appoint a full-time Muslim halal supervisor, among other requirements (The Straits Times).

Muslim-owned tells you who owns the business, not whether it is certified. Malaysia's certification looks at ingredients, process and safety rather than ownership, and JAKIM dismissed a 2022 proposal for logos coloured by who owns the business (The Straits Times). A Muslim-owned restaurant without a certificate will not be in the directory, so ask the staff where their meat comes from.

No pork no lard, "pork free" and "Muslim friendly" are signs restaurants put up themselves, and they do not represent formal certification (The Straits Times). They tell you there is no pork. They do not tell you how the chicken or beef was slaughtered. In November 2025 JAKIM also said it had never recognised a private "Muslim Choice" label (The Straits Times).
Decide before you land which of these you are comfortable with, so you are not deciding at the door.
How to check a restaurant in the Halal Malaysia directory

Open halal.gov.my on your phone and find the Verify Halal Status box. Choose the category Premis Makanan (food premises), type the restaurant or brand name and search. The Premis Makanan results list each outlet with its name, the company behind it, its address, its brand and the certificate's expiry date (Halal Malaysia directory).

Certificates belong to an outlet, so one branch can be listed while another is not. Match the address to the place you are standing in, and check that the expiry date has not passed. Look for a status note too: one Penang listing we saw today was marked "Sijil Telah Ditarik Balik", which means the certificate has been withdrawn (Halal Malaysia directory).

Keep searches short. The directory matches the name it holds, which may not be the name on the sign. "Seirock" found every Ramen Seirock-Ya outlet; "Din Tai Fung" found nothing today. If nothing comes up, ask at the counter to see the certificate and read the name and expiry date on it.
A checked example: Ramen Seirock-Ya

Ramen Seirock-Ya is in the Teeko directory, and its own listing says it is halal certified. The listing describes a ramen chain from Japan with branches in Japan, Malaysia and Indonesia, a signature Toripaitan-style ramen, and the words "Halal certified". Its address is 6-G Jalan SS 21/35, Damansara Utama, in Petaling Jaya.

We checked. The Halal Malaysia directory lists Joypack Foods Malaysia Sdn. Bhd., with the website seirock-ya.com.my, at Jalan SS21/35, Damansara Utama, along with certified menu items such as Fish Toripaitan ramen and chicken gyoza (Halal Malaysia directory). It also lists Ramen Seirock-Ya outlets inside KL: Level 5 of NU Sentral, Level 2 of Intermark Mall on Jalan Tun Razak, and Level G of MyTown Shopping Centre on Jalan Cochrane (Halal Malaysia directory). For more bowls, read the halal ramen in KL guide.
Search the outlet you plan to visit before you go. Expiry dates differ from branch to branch.
Masjid India and Jalan TAR

Two listings on Jalan Masjid India call themselves halal on Google Maps. Zafaran de' cafe is at No.05, next to Mydin, 11 Jalan Masjid India, and Restoran Al Bidayah is at 83 Jalan Masjid India. Both are listed as halal restaurants by the business. Neither came up when we searched their names in the directory today, so look for the JAKIM certificate at the counter.

Kompleks Sogo, at 190 Jalan Tuanku Abdul Rahman (Jalan TAR), has both kinds under one roof. Squid Boy @ Sogo KL, at LG-K8 on the Lower Ground Floor, lists itself as halal on Google Maps, with fried chicken, Japanese and Taiwanese categories. It was not in the directory under that name today. The directory does list other outlets in the building, including Nando's and The Chicken Rice Shop on Level 6 and Secret Recipe on the ground floor (Halal Malaysia directory).
Want a certified meal here without searching? Take the escalator to Level 6 of Sogo.
KLCC and Jalan Ampang

Level 4 of Suria KLCC shows the difference on one floor. DIN by Din Tai Fung at Suria KLCC [No Pork No Lard], at Lot 417 and 417A, puts "No Pork No Lard" in its Google Maps name and is listed as a Taiwanese and Chinese restaurant. That is the restaurant's own description, and its name did not come up in the directory today. On the same floor, Cili Kampung at Lot 432 to 433 is listed in the Halal Malaysia directory (Halal Malaysia directory). Search "suria klcc" in the directory and you will see more certified outlets in the mall.

On Jalan Ampang, Dara Grill Burger (Auntie B'S Kopitiam) at L7.06, Wisma Central lists itself as halal on Google Maps. For ramen near KLCC, the directory lists Ramen Seirock-Ya at Intermark Mall, 348 Jalan Tun Razak (Halal Malaysia directory).
Search the mall name in the directory before you go. It is quicker than walking the floors.
Chinatown

Jalan Sultan has two hot pot listings with halal labels. TIANFU Chinese Muslim HOTPOT, on the 1st Floor of 66-68 Jalan Sultan, is listed on Google Maps as a halal restaurant and calls itself Chinese Muslim in its name. Ma La Tang Halal Spicy Hot Pot, at 72 Jalan Sultan, is listed as a Chinese restaurant with halal in its name. Neither came up in the directory under those names today.

Restoran Yusoof & Zakhir on Jalan Hang Kasturi is listed on Google Maps as an Indian Muslim restaurant. That describes the kitchen style, not a certificate. For a directory-listed stop on the same road, Central Market Annexe on Jalan Hang Kasturi has Secret Recipe on the ground floor and a Koppiku coffee outlet (Halal Malaysia directory).
At the Jalan Sultan hot pot places, ask to see the certificate before you order.
Bukit Bintang

Central City Bistro, on Level 1 at 38 Jalan Pudu, and Restoran Nan Indah on Jalan Imbi both list themselves as halal restaurants on Google Maps. Neither was in the directory under those names today. On Jalan Sultan Ismail, the directory lists Halab Gate Shawarma at 51-1 and 51-2 (Halal Malaysia directory).
Heading to Jalan Alor, the food street nearby? The Jalan Alor food guide explains how halal works there, and the Bukit Bintang food guide covers the malls. Read both before your first evening out.
From KLIA2 to halal food in KL
Hungry before you leave the airport? KLIA2 has outlets that list themselves as halal, and the KLIA2 food guide covers where they are. The same checks apply there.

The bus from KLIA2 to KL Sentral ends at KL Sentral (ttklia.com). NU Sentral connects with KL Sentral and opens 10am to 10pm daily (NU Sentral), and the directory lists Ramen Seirock-Ya on its Level 5 (Halal Malaysia directory). The fare is shown on the booking page.

Frequently Asked Questions
How do I know if a restaurant in KL is halal?

Look for the JAKIM halal logo and certificate, then search the restaurant under Premis Makanan in the Verify Halal Status box on halal.gov.my. Check that the outlet address matches and the expiry date has not passed (Halal Malaysia directory).
Is no pork no lard the same as halal?
No. "No pork no lard" is the restaurant's own sign and does not represent formal certification (The Straits Times). It does not tell you how the meat was slaughtered.
Is a Muslim-owned restaurant halal certified?
Not automatically. Malaysia's halal certification looks at ingredients and process, not ownership (The Straits Times). Search the directory or ask to see the certificate.
Is all food in KL halal?
No. Not every outlet in Malaysia is willing or able to pay for certification, and some put up their own labels instead (The Straits Times). Check each restaurant.
Where can I find halal food near KL Sentral?
NU Sentral, which connects with KL Sentral, has Ramen Seirock-Ya on Level 5, listed in the Halal Malaysia directory (Halal Malaysia directory, NU Sentral). The mall opens 10am to 10pm.
Conclusion

Halal food in KL is easy to check once you know the logo and the directory. Search the outlet on halal.gov.my, read the address and expiry date, and treat "no pork no lard" as a description, not a certificate. The Google Maps listings here are a snapshot, so open each link to check opening hours before you go. Landing at KLIA2? Book the bus from KLIA2 to KL Sentral on ttklia.com and have your first halal meal at NU Sentral.
